Theme 098 · Camera & edit grammar

Dolly Zoom

Hitchcock’s vertigo shot as a product moment. The anomaly card stays exactly the same size in the middle of the frame while the camera dollies in and the lens zooms out, so the wall of dashboards behind it stretches into a tunnel: the feeling of “something is wrong” made physical. Lens and dolly sliders in a HUD show the two opposing moves in every still.

COMPONENT KIT

  • Dashboard wall / tunnel — the background that stretches; built as a 4-wall CSS 3D box
  • Locked subject — the anomaly card, which never changes size or position during the move
  • Subject bracket — amber bracket that picks the one tile that matters out of the wall
  • Lens + dolly HUD — two sliders moving in opposite directions, explaining the effect in a still
  • FOV guides — nested dashed rectangles showing the background field of view shrinking
  • Opposing arrows — DOLLY IN → / ← ZOOM OUT marks under the subject

MOTION · MUSIC

  • Zolly — perspective 1400 → 420 px while the tunnel translates z −800 px, over 2 bars (4 s at 120 BPM) with sine.inOut; subject scale compensates to stay constant
  • Drop push — straight scale 1 → 1.12 in 0.3 s (expo.out) exactly on the drop; frame guides scale 1.4 → 1 staggered 0.08 s
  • Release — zolly reverses in 1 bar with power2.out; background desaturates back to navy; tagline lines on beats 1 and 3

WHY / RISK · ADAPT IT

The dolly zoom is the cinema shorthand for a sudden realisation, which is exactly the moment an anomaly is caught. Holding the card steady while the world warps makes the one metric feel like the only thing that matters. Risk: it’s disorienting and expensive to do properly; use it once, on the proof beat only.

Adapt to your product: Choose the single object your product surfaces (an alert, a failing test, a fraud flag, a lead score) as the locked subject, and use the screens your users stare at today as the stretching background. Everything else in the film should be calm so the zolly lands.
